workshop.title: Workshop
workshop.open_tip: Instruments to print and make, computed for the place
workshop.intro: Instruments to print at true scale, cut out and assemble, computed for {place}. Change the place, the time zone or the date below without touching the side panel. Each PDF ends with sheets: assembly, use, the astronomy behind it, computed examples.
workshop.saved: {path} saved ({pages} pages). Print at 100 %, without “fit to page”, and check the 100 mm ruler.
workshop.latitude_range: The Workshop's instruments are computed between 10° and 80° of latitude (north or south).
workshop.desc_planisphere: Planisphere: a disc of the stars to magnitude 4.5 and the 88 constellations, under a mask whose window is the horizon of your latitude. Set the date against the hour: the window shows the sky. Easy.
workshop.desc_equatorial_dial: Equatorial sundial: a dial parallel to the equator, a rod pointing at the pole, even hours 15° apart, already corrected for your longitude. Two faces (spring–summer, autumn–winter) and two wedges. Easy.
workshop.desc_horizontal_dial: Horizontal sundial: the hour lines of your latitude and longitude, the curves of the solstices and equinoxes traced by the gnomon's nodus. Easy.
workshop.correction_title: From the dial's time to the legal time
workshop.no_summer: Your time zone has no summer time: set the legal time directly.
workshop.planisphere_disc_hint: Cut along the thick line, pierce the small cross at the centre.
workshop.planisphere_mask_hint: Cut out the circle, cut away the grey window, pierce the centre. Or print this page on a transparent sheet.
workshop.planisphere_mask_time: Hours of the {zone} time zone (standard time)
workshop.planisphere_mask_summer: In summer time, set one hour earlier
workshop.planisphere_what: A planisphere (star wheel) shows the sky visible at any date and any hour. The star disc turns under a fixed mask; the mask's window is the horizon of your place, so only the stars that are up appear in it. It is computed for your latitude (the shape of the window) and for your longitude (where the dates fall against the hours): a planisphere from a shop, made for an average latitude and the time zone's meridian, is off by several minutes and a few degrees.
workshop.planisphere_assembly:
Materials: thin card of 200 to 300 g/m² (or thick paper glued on the card of a cereal box), a split pin, scissors and a craft knife. Optionally, a transparent sheet for the mask.
1. Print at 100 % and check the 100 mm ruler at the bottom of each page.
2. Cut out the star disc along the thick outer line.
3. Cut out the mask, then cut away the window (the grey area) with the knife. Printed on a transparent sheet, the mask needs no cutting inside.
4. Pierce both centres, lay the mask on the disc and join them with the split pin. The disc should turn without play.
workshop.planisphere_use: Turn the disc to bring today's date (the disc's outer ring) against the hour (the mask's ring). The window then shows the sky at that moment: its edge is the horizon, the cross the zenith (the point above your head), the dotted curves the altitudes of 30° and 60°. Hold the map above your head, the letter of the direction you face at the bottom: the stars at the bottom of the window are then low on the horizon in front of you. That is why east is on the left: the map reads like the sky seen from below.
workshop.planisphere_use_2: Other uses: to know when a star rises, bring it to the east edge of the window and read the hour against the date; the same on the west edge for its setting, and on the vertical line from the centre down (the meridian) for its highest point. The planets, the Moon and comets move among the stars and are not printed: take their right ascension and declination from Céleste's Coordinates tab and mark them in pencil on the disc, using the hours of right ascension around the star field and the ecliptic (dashed), on which the Sun and the planets stay.
workshop.planisphere_summer: The mask's hours are the time zone's standard (winter) time. In summer time, take one hour off before setting: at 23:00 in summer, set 22:00.
workshop.planisphere_example: On {date} at {legal} (legal time), set {hour} against the date. Céleste computes for that moment the highest bright stars above 10° of altitude: {stars}. You should find them in the window, at those altitudes and in those directions.
workshop.planisphere_astro: The projection: the celestial pole is at the centre, and the declinations lie at distances from the centre proportional to their distance from the pole (azimuthal equidistant projection). The disc reaches declination {edge}°, a little beyond the horizon of your latitude ({lat}°): the stars nearer the other pole never rise where you are. The farther from the centre, the more the figures are stretched sideways: the price of any flat map of the sky. The date ring gives, for each day of {year} at 0:00 (standard time of the {zone} zone), the local sidereal time at your longitude ({lon}°); your mean solar time differs from the zone's time by {shift} min, and the ring takes it into account.
workshop.planisphere_astro_2: Why the date turns against the hour: the Earth turns once relative to the stars in 23 h 56 min 4 s (the sidereal day), four minutes less than the solar day, because it also moves along its orbit. Each evening the stars rise four minutes earlier, two hours a month: the sky of 22:00 in January is that of 20:00 in February. Accuracy: a few minutes of time and one or two degrees of position. The stars are placed for the year 2000; the precession of the Earth's axis moves them by a degree in 72 years, which gives the map decades of use (the date ring slips by a minute in four years, with the leap years).
workshop.equatorial_stand: Equatorial sundial — wedges of the stand
workshop.equatorial_summer_dates: lit from the spring equinox to the autumn equinox
workshop.equatorial_winter_dates: lit from the autumn equinox to the spring equinox
workshop.equatorial_what: The equatorial sundial is the simplest of sundials, and the one that explains itself: its dial is parallel to the celestial equator and its rod parallel to the Earth's axis, pointing at the celestial pole (near the Pole Star in the northern hemisphere). The Sun turns around the rod at 15° an hour: the hour lines are evenly spaced. It lights the upper face during the half of the year when it is on the side of the visible pole (from spring to autumn), and the lower face in the other half; at the equinoxes it grazes the dial.
workshop.equatorial_assembly:
Materials: stiff card or 3 mm plywood, a straight rod (a skewer, a bicycle spoke) of 8 to 10 cm, glue, a small board as a base.
1. Print at 100 % and cut out both faces. Glue them back to back on the card, the “top” marks together: the two noon lines must lie on each other (look through against the light).
2. Pierce the centre and push the rod through, square to the dial, leaving 4 to 5 cm on each side.
3. Cut out the two wedges, fold their tabs and glue them on the base, parallel and as far apart as the dial is wide. Lay the dial on their slanted edges, the “top” side up: the dial then makes {tilt}° with the horizontal and the rod rises at {rod}° (your latitude) towards the pole.
workshop.sundial_orientation: The dial must face true (geographic) north, not magnetic north: a compass is off by the place's magnetic declination (a few degrees in Europe, much more elsewhere). Most accurate: at the Sun's meridian transit given by Céleste (its culmination, in the Ephemeris tab), the shadow of a plumb line traces the north–south line; mark it on the ground. Lay the dial's noon line on it, the rod or the gnomon pointing at the visible pole (north in the northern hemisphere).
workshop.equatorial_use: Read the hour on the line where the rod's shadow falls, on the lit face. These hours are your time zone's standard time, already corrected for your longitude: only the equation of time remains (table below) and, in summer, an hour to add. For a few days around the equinoxes the Sun grazes the dial and the shadow is blurred: that is normal, and even the proof that the dial is parallel to the equator.
workshop.sundial_corrections: Legal time = time read on the dial + the table's correction (+ 1 h in summer time). The correction is the opposite of the equation of time: the true Sun runs up to 16 minutes ahead of the mean Sun in early November and 14 minutes behind in mid-February, because the Earth's orbit is an ellipse (it moves faster in January) and its axis is tilted on the orbit. Corrections in minutes, on the 1st, 11th and 21st of each month:
workshop.sundial_example: On {date} at {legal} (legal time), the shadow should fall on {reading}: equation of time {eot} min, summer time {dst} h. Check it on that day, or compare at any time with the Sun's culmination given by Céleste: at that moment the shadow is on the noon line.
workshop.equatorial_astro: Why it works: seen from the Earth, the Sun draws each day a circle parallel to the celestial equator, around the axis of the sky, at an even 15° an hour. A rod parallel to that axis, on a dial parallel to the equator (tilted by the complement of your latitude, {lat}°), casts a shadow that therefore turns by 15° an hour whatever the season. Only the shadow's length changes with the Sun's declination: long near the equinoxes, shorter at the solstices.
workshop.sundial_longitude: The longitude correction: the time of the {zone} zone is the mean time of a reference meridian; at your longitude ({lon}°) the mean solar time differs from it by {shift} min (4 minutes per degree). The hour lines are already shifted by as much: the dial is engraved for your place, not for another town of the same region.
workshop.horizontal_gnomon_sizes: Height of the nodus: {height} mm · base: {base} mm · edge: {style} mm
workshop.horizontal_what: The horizontal sundial is the garden sundial: a horizontal dial and a triangular gnomon whose edge points at the celestial pole, rising at the angle of your latitude. The hour lines are not even: close together around noon, wide apart in the morning and the evening. The top of the gnomon carries a nodus (a notch), whose shadow follows each day a date curve: the June solstice, the equinoxes (a straight line), the December solstice, and between them the dates when the Sun enters the signs of the zodiac (dotted).
workshop.horizontal_assembly:
Materials: stiff card, plywood or thin metal for the gnomon; a flat board for the dial; glue.
1. Print at 100 % and check the 100 mm ruler. Glue the dial on a stiff, flat support.
2. Cut out the gnomon (the triangle and its tab), fold the tab and glue the gnomon upright on the dial's thick line: the sharp angle on the foot of the gnomon, the nodus straight above the “nodus” mark.
3. Check with a set square that the gnomon is vertical, and that its slanted edge rises towards the visible pole (north in the northern hemisphere).
workshop.horizontal_level: The dial must be exactly horizontal: check it with a spirit level in two directions. An error of one degree shifts the hours by a few minutes.
workshop.horizontal_use: Read the hour on the line where the shadow of the gnomon's edge falls (the half hours are the short marks at the edge). The tip of the nodus' shadow gives the date to within a few days: on the equinox line in late March and late September, on the curve nearest the foot at the June solstice (the farthest in the southern hemisphere), on the farthest at the December solstice.
workshop.horizontal_astro: Why the hours are uneven: the gnomon's edge is parallel to the Earth's axis, like the rod of the equatorial dial; its shadow turns evenly by 15° an hour in the plane of the equator. Projected on a horizontal dial, this even turn gives each line an angle θ from the noon line: tan θ = sin φ · tan H, where φ = {lat}° is your latitude and H the Sun's hour angle (15° an hour from solar noon). The nodus traces the date curves: over a day, at a fixed declination, the shadow of a point draws a conic on the plane — a hyperbola at our latitudes, a straight line at the equinoxes, when the Sun stays in the plane of the equator.
workshop.desc_astrolabe: A complete planispheric astrolabe: the mater and its limb (hours and degrees), the plate of your latitude (almucantars every 5°, azimuths, twilight, unequal hours), the rete with the stars of the year to print on a transparent sheet, the rule, the back (altitudes, zodiac, calendar, shadow square) and the alidade. Demanding.
workshop.desc_nocturnal: Nocturnal: the time at night from the stars turning round the pole (the Great Bear or the Little Bear in the north, the Southern Cross in the south), its date disc set for your longitude. Medium.

workshop.astrolabe_what: The planispheric astrolabe was the “calculating machine” of the astronomers of the Middle Ages and the Renaissance. It shows the vault of the sky flat, by stereographic projection from the south celestial pole onto the plane of the equator. The plate, engraved for one latitude, carries the lines of the local sky: horizon, circles of altitude (almucantars), azimuths. The rete, open-worked (here transparent), carries the moving sky: the ecliptic, along which the Sun runs, and the bright stars. Turning it as the sky turns, you read the time, the risings and settings, the length of the day, the position of any star. The back, with the alidade, measures the altitude of the stars and of buildings.
workshop.astrolabe_assembly:
Materials: thick card (300 g/m², or grey board of 1 to 2 mm), a transparent sheet for printers, a split pin (or a 3 mm screw and nut), glue, a string for the ring.
1. Print at 100 % and check the 100 mm ruler. Print the page of the rete and the rule on the transparent sheet.
2. Glue the front and the back on stiff card, back to back, the thrones on each other (push a needle through both centres to align them). Cut along the outline.
3. Cut the rete (the circle) and the rule from the transparent sheet, and the alidade from card; fold the alidade's vanes at a right angle.
4. Stack, from the back to the front: the alidade, the mater, the rete, the rule. Pass the split pin through the four centres. The rete and the rule must turn freely; the alidade too, on the back.
5. Tie a string through the hole of the throne: hanging from it, the astrolabe stays vertical for the measurements.
workshop.astrolabe_parts:
• The limb (edge of the front): the apparent solar time, noon at the top, midnight at the bottom, every 5 minutes; inside, the degrees from 0 to 360°, counted from the meridian.
• The plate: the horizon (thick line), the almucantars every 5° (figures along the meridian), the azimuths every 15° (figures near the horizon, 0° north), the zenith (cross), the line of astronomical twilight (Sun 18° below the horizon, dashed), the unequal hours below the horizon (dotted), the tropics and the equator.
• The rete: the ecliptic, graduated degree by degree in each sign of the zodiac, and the bright stars brought to the year, each at the tip of a small arrow.
• The rule: its middle line passes through the centre; it carries the scale of declinations (−20° to +20°, and the tropics).
• The back: the altitude scale (0° horizontal, 90° at the top), the zodiac, the calendar of the year (the date gives the Sun's longitude), the shadow square.
workshop.astrolabe_measure: Hold the astrolabe by its ring, vertical, the back towards you. For a star, sight it through both holes of the vanes, turning the alidade; for the Sun, never look at it: turn the alidade until the ray through the hole of the upper vane falls on the hole of the lower one. The tip of the alidade shows the altitude on the scale of the edge. The shadow square gives the height of a building: sight its top; below 45°, height = distance × umbra versa reading ÷ 12; above, height = distance × 12 ÷ umbra recta reading (add the height of your eyes).
workshop.astrolabe_use:
Reading the time by day:
1. On the back, lay the alidade on the date: it shows on the zodiac the Sun's longitude (for example 20° of Scorpio).
2. Measure the Sun's altitude.
3. On the front, turn the rete until the point of the ecliptic where the Sun is lies on the almucantar of that altitude, on the east side in the morning, the west in the afternoon.
4. Lay the rule over that point: its end shows the apparent solar time on the limb.
Reading the time at night: measure the altitude of a star of the rete, bring its tip onto the almucantar of that altitude (on the right side of the meridian), then lay the rule over the Sun's point, below the horizon: the limb gives the time.
workshop.astrolabe_use_2: Other uses: the sunrise (its point on the horizon, Rising side) and the sunset (Setting side), hence the length of the day; the start and the end of the full night (its point on the twilight line); the azimuth of a body (the azimuth line under its tip); the stars visible at a given hour (those above the horizon); the unequal hour of the Ancients (lay the point of the ecliptic opposite the Sun on the hour lines). The degree of the limb under the meridian, the rete set, gives the sidereal time.
workshop.astrolabe_time_title: From apparent solar time to legal time
workshop.astrolabe_time: The limb gives the apparent solar time of the place: noon when the Sun crosses the meridian. For the legal time of the {zone} zone: add the correction of the equation of time (table below), then {shift} min for your longitude, and 1 h in summer time.
workshop.astrolabe_example_day: On {date} at {legal} (legal time), Céleste computes the Sun at {alt}° of altitude, {side}. On the back, the date is against {lon}° of {sign}. Lay that point of the ecliptic on the almucantar of {alt}° {side}: the rule shows {reading} on the limb. Check: {reading} − ({eot} min) + ({shift} min) + {dst} h ≈ {legal}.
workshop.astrolabe_example_night: The same evening at {legal}, {star} is {alt}° high, {side}. Bring its tip onto the almucantar of {alt}° {side} and lay the rule over the Sun's point (below the horizon): the limb shows {reading}, the apparent solar time of {legal}.
workshop.astrolabe_astro: The stereographic projection, known to Hipparchus and Ptolemy, has two properties that make the astrolabe possible: it turns every circle of the sphere into a circle (or a straight line) on the plane, and it keeps the angles. The almucantars, the azimuths, the ecliptic are therefore drawn with compasses. The equator is the circle of radius 1, the tropic of Cancer that of radius tan(45° − ε/2), the tropic of Capricorn, the edge of the plate, that of radius tan(45° + ε/2), ε = 23.44° being the obliquity of the ecliptic. The zenith is tan((90° − φ)/2) from the centre, φ = {lat}° being your latitude: it gives the plate its shape, hence one plate per latitude.
workshop.astrolabe_astro_2: Turning the rete turns the sky round the axis of the world: once per sidereal day (23 h 56 min). The Sun moves about a degree a day along the ecliptic, which the calendar of the back turns into a longitude, computed by Céleste for each day of the year. The stars are placed for the year of the instrument: precession moves them by a degree in 72 years, which is why old astrolabes, engraved for their time, are no longer quite right today. Accuracy of a card astrolabe: a few minutes of time, one or two degrees of altitude.

workshop.nocturnal_hours_hint: Thick card. Cut out the hour disc (with its teeth) and the arm, pierce their centres at 5 mm.
workshop.nocturnal_arm: arm: lay its edge along the pointer stars
workshop.nocturnal_what: The nocturnal was the instrument of sailors and travellers from the 16th to the 18th century to know the time at night. All the stars turn round the Pole Star, close to the pole, in a sidereal day: the direction of a star seen from the Pole Star is the hand of a sky clock. The “guards” are used: Dubhe, one of the two stars at the edge of the pan of the Great Bear (tooth GB), or Kochab, the brightest of the bowl of the Little Bear (tooth LB). The date disc, set for your longitude, corrects the stars' four minutes of advance a day.
workshop.nocturnal_what_south: The nocturnal was the instrument of sailors and travellers to know the time at night. All the stars turn round the celestial pole in a sidereal day: the direction of a star seen from the pole is the hand of a sky clock. In the southern sky, without a pole star, the Southern Cross is used: its long axis, from Gacrux to Acrux, points to the south celestial pole, about four and a half times its length beyond Acrux. The date disc, set for your longitude, corrects the stars' four minutes of advance a day.
workshop.nocturnal_assembly:
Materials: thick card, a 5 mm eyelet or hollow rivet (or a split pin and a hole a little off centre), glue.
1. Print at 100 % and check the 100 mm ruler. Glue the pages on card and cut out the three parts.
2. Pierce the three centres with a 5 mm hole.
3. Stack the date disc (below), the hour disc, then the arm, and join them with the eyelet: you must see the sky through it. The two discs and the arm turn independently.
workshop.nocturnal_use:
1. Turn the hour disc to put tooth GB on today's date (or tooth LB if you use Kochab).
2. Hold the nocturnal by the handle, at arm's length, upright, facing north, the handle down.
3. Sight the Pole Star through the hole at the centre.
4. Turn the arm until its edge passes through Dubhe and Merak, the two stars at the edge of the pan (or through Kochab).
5. Read the time where the arm crosses the hour disc.
workshop.nocturnal_use_south:
1. Turn the hour disc to put the “Cross” tooth on today's date.
2. Hold the nocturnal by the handle, at arm's length, upright, facing south, the handle down.
3. Sight the south celestial pole through the hole at the centre (extend the long axis of the Cross four and a half times its length beyond Acrux).
4. Turn the arm until its edge passes through Gacrux and Acrux.
5. Read the time where the arm crosses the hour disc.
workshop.nocturnal_summer: The hours of the disc are the time zone's standard time. In summer time, add an hour to the reading.
workshop.nocturnal_example: On {date} at {legal} (legal time), Céleste places {star} so that the arm points to {clock} o'clock on a clock face, seen from the front. The hour disc should then show {hour} (standard time).
workshop.nocturnal_astro: The date disc carries, for each day of {year}, the position of the pointer star at 0:00 (standard time of the {zone} zone) seen from your longitude ({lon}°): its hour angle at midnight, which falls back by 3 min 56 s a day, two hours a month. The hour disc graduates mean time at the speed of the sky, 15.04° an hour. So, when the tooth is on the date, the arm laid on the star shows the zone's time directly.
workshop.nocturnal_astro_2: Accuracy: the Pole Star is not exactly at the pole, it is 0.65° from it (and comes closer until 2100); sighting the Pole Star instead of the pole shifts the reading by a few minutes depending on the hour. With a card instrument held by hand, count a quarter of an hour. Sailors used it to know the hour of the watches and of the tide.
workshop.nocturnal_astro_south: Accuracy: no bright star marks the south celestial pole; sighting its estimated place and the line of the Cross limits the reading to about a quarter of an hour. The Cross stays above the horizon all night only south of 34° of latitude; elsewhere it can be used only part of the year.
